text: Cash the company pays to shareholders, per share, from its payment record. A buyer has to own the stock before the ex-dividend date to receive the next payment, and the price usually drops by about the dividend on that date.

A split changes how many shares exist without changing what the company is worth: a 2-for-1 split doubles the shares and halves the price. Past prices are adjusted for splits, so charts compare like with like.

The company's latest filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission: annual reports (10-K), quarterly reports (10-Q) and notices of material events (8-K), among others. They are the primary source most of the figures elsewhere are drawn from.

Who is trading what and who the government is paying, from three public filing regimes: company insiders' Form 4s, members of the House under the STOCK Act, and federal contract awards. Each is published after a delay, and nothing here is ranked by how profitable it looked.

Which widely followed companies report between Monday and Friday of this week, grouped by day, with the names on your own watchlist marked. It scans a fixed list of widely followed names, not the whole market, because free data gives one earnings date per symbol at a time.

Today's price against three yardsticks on one axis: the range the company's own price-to-earnings history implies, the analysts' price targets, and its trading range over the past year. Each shows a range rather than a single figure, because none of them is precise.
The stock's daily closing price over the last twelve months, with its earnings reports, ex-dividend dates and splits marked on it. It shows how the price moved and what it did around each event.

Each compared name's price over the past year, rebased so that all of them start at 100 on the same day. A line ending at 130 has risen 30 percent over the period, so the ends can be compared directly.

Official US economic series from the Federal Reserve's FRED database, such as inflation, jobs, spending and output, shown in the form each is usually read in. Their releases are among the main scheduled movers of rates and stocks.
The gap between the best bid and the best ask, as a percentage of the mid price. Wider spreads cost more to get in and out of.
How much the sector has gained or lost against the benchmark over the past
, as the change in the ratio of its price to the benchmark's, in percent. Positive means it has outpaced the index, whatever either did on its own.
The compound annual growth rate over
years: the steady yearly return that would turn the starting value into the ending one. It smooths the path, so two series with the same figure can have had very different rides.
Where the price sits against its 200-day moving average, in percent. The 200-day is the most watched long-term trend line, and trading above it is how a long-term uptrend usually looks.
Where the price sits against its 50-day moving average, in percent. Positive means it trades above the average, which is how a medium-term uptrend usually looks.
Where the price sits against its 40-week moving average, in percent. Forty weeks is close to the 200-day average, measured on weekly closes, which smooths out single-day noise.

Where the price sits against its 200-week moving average, about four years of weekly closes, in percent. It is the slowest trend line in common use, so a price far above it has run well ahead of its long-run trend.
The 14-period RSI computed on weekly closes, from 0 to 100. Above 70 means weeks of hard buying and below 30 weeks of hard selling, on a slower clock than the daily reading.
How far the ratio sits from its own 60-session average, measured in standard deviations. Beyond plus or minus 2 is unusually stretched for that pair, the zone a mean-reversion trade looks for.
The volatility the option's price implies, annualised and in percent: how much movement the market is paying for. Higher implied volatility makes options dearer for buyers and pays sellers more.
Open interest: how many contracts at this strike and expiry are still open, counted after the previous session. It shows where positions sit, not how much traded today.
How far the price stands below its highest close so far, in percent. Zero means it is at a high, and minus 30 means it would need to rise about 43 percent to get back.
The deepest fall from a high to a later low over the history measured, in percent. It is the loss someone who bought at the worst moment would have sat through before any recovery.
The price of the level, with whether it sits below the current price as support or above it as resistance. Levels come from where price has repeatedly turned.
How far this level sits from the current price, as a percentage. Negative means the level is below the stock, positive that it is above.

A 0-100 score for how much this level has actually mattered: how many pivots cluster there, how firmly price was rejected, how much volume traded across it, and how recently it was last defended. A high score is a level the market has kept respecting, not one it must respect again.
How many separate times price reversed at this level, and how long ago it was last tested. More touches means more traders are watching it; a level untouched for a long time matters less.

The Fibonacci retracement this line is drawn at, as a share of the swing it measures; 38.2%, 50% and 61.8% are the ones traders watch most. A pullback that holds near one is commonly read as the trend resuming.
How far this level sits from the current price, as a percentage. Negative means the level is below the stock, positive that it is above.
Whether this level sits below the current price, as support and a potential floor, or above it, as resistance and a potential ceiling. A level can change roles once price closes through it.
The average's current value, in dollars: the mean of the closes over its window. A price above it is trading above its recent norm.
Where the stock is trading against that average, as a percentage. Positive means the price is above the average, negative that it is below.
Whether the average itself is rising or falling over the last ten days. The direction of the trend, not just where price sits.

Which options level the row is: the call and put walls, where dealer gamma is heaviest above and below the price, the gamma pin, where it is heaviest overall, and the strike with the most open interest. These are the prices dealer hedging tends to lean against.

text: How far the level sits from the current price, as a percentage. Negative means it is below the stock, positive that it is above.

The dealers' gamma at that strike, in dollars of delta for a 1 percent move in the stock, under the sign convention stated below. Positive gamma tends to damp moves near the level and negative gamma to add to them.
Whether the contract is a call, which gains as the stock rises, or a put, which gains as it falls. Either can be bought or sold, so the type alone does not say which way the trade is betting.
The rank line the stock crossed: 80 marks the top fifth of its peers and 20 the bottom fifth. Up through 80 is a name starting to lead; down through 20, one starting to lag.
Its percentile rank among its 143 peers on the day it crossed, from 0 to 100. A rank of 97 means it beat 97 percent of them over the window.
What the zone is drawn from: the 40-week or 200-week average, or a retracement of the past three years' range. These are the prices long-term buyers have tended to step in at before.
How far the zone sits from the current price, as a percentage. Negative means it is below the stock, positive that it is above.
Support when the zone is below the price; resistance, or a level to reclaim for an average, when it is above. It says where the level sits, not that it will hold.
The dollar value of the transaction as filed: the shares times the price reported on the Form 4. A grant or an exercise can carry a price of zero or one that is not a market price.

Which way the trade needs the stock to go. Bullish makes money as the stock rises, bearish as it falls. A bought put is a bearish bet even though the contract itself is owned, which is why the direction is spelled out rather than left as long or short.
The price the position was opened at, and underneath it the latest price it is marked at. For an option both are premium per share, not the share price.

How far the stock has travelled along the line between the stop and the target. The small tick is where the trade opened, the dot is where the stock is now, and the shaded stretch between them is the ground it has covered.
Profit or loss at the latest mark, in dollars and as a percentage of what was paid. Nothing is settled until the position closes, so treat every figure here as provisional.
The loss this position was sized to take if the stop is hit. It was decided before the trade opened, which is what makes the total risk on the page a real ceiling rather than an estimate.

How strongly the scan rated this setup when it opened, out of 100. Shown as strength only. The direction it was rating is the Betting on column, so a bearish 44 and a bullish 44 both read as 44 here rather than one of them as minus 44. It is a record of why the trade was taken, not a live reading: it is not recalculated as the position runs.

Which entry rule the row is, such as a breakout above a range or a pullback to an average, read on completed candles. Each arms on its setup, triggers on one exact candle event and is cancelled by its invalidation level.

A blend of relative strength against the benchmark from one week to six months, weighted toward one to three months, plus a few points for trend confirmation: price above its 50 and 200-day averages and the ratio line above its own. Higher means stronger leadership.
The composite read as a word: strong at 8 or more, improving from 2, neutral in between, deteriorating from minus 2 and weak at minus 8 or below. It names the reading and adds nothing to it.

A 0 to 100 score for how close the basket is to a breakout: near its 20-day or three-month high, its Bollinger bands squeezed, momentum firm without being stretched, and volume picking up. It is high only when those line up, because any one alone is noise.
The first leg's price divided by the second's. A rising ratio means the first is outperforming the second, whatever the market as a whole did.
The reasoning behind the pair: why one side might outperform the other, such as industrials over staples or miners over the market. It is the idea the ratio tests, not a forecast.

What this table's rules call the ratio's reading: a z-score beyond plus or minus 2 is a mean-reversion setup, and a ratio trending above its 50-day average a momentum setup. It names the reading; it is not an instruction.

Where the sector sits on the rotation chart: leading is strong and still gaining, weakening is strong but losing ground, lagging is weak and losing, and improving is weak but gaining. Sectors tend to pass through them clockwise.
The sector's performance against the benchmark compared with its own recent norm, centred on 100 and measured on weekly bars. Above 100 means it is outperforming by more than usual for it.
Whether the sector's relative strength is rising or falling, centred on 100. Above 100 means it is gaining ground on the benchmark, and below 100 means it is losing ground.
How much the strength reading changed over the latest week. A positive figure is a sector moving right on the rotation chart, toward leading or weakening.
How much the momentum reading changed over the latest week. A positive figure is a sector moving up on the rotation chart, toward improving or leading.

The quadrant the sector was in a week earlier, shown only when it has crossed into a new one. A crossing is the earliest thing the chart says and also the least reliable, since a sector near a line can cross back.

The information coefficient of the screen's own score at this horizon: the rank correlation between each name's score and its later return against the rest of the universe, averaged across dates. Zero means the score is noise, and real equity signals tend to sit around 0.02 to 0.05.
The same measurement for a score made of random numbers, the control for luck. A composite that does not clear it by a margin has shown nothing.
The same measurement for one raw factor, the past three months' return on its own. A blended score has to beat this to justify its extra parts.
Whether the composite's coefficient beats the three-month return's at this horizon. Losing means the plain past return ranked the names at least as well as the whole score did.
The band of scores the observations fell in, from strongly negative to strongly positive. Each row collects every name that scored in that band on any evaluation date.
How many observations fall in the bucket, one for each name on each date it scored there. The observations overlap in time, so they are less independent than the count suggests.
The average return over the horizon after subtracting the whole universe's average for the same dates. Positive means names in this bucket beat the other names on the same days.
The share of observations in the bucket whose excess return was above zero. Fifty percent is what a coin would manage.

The range that would hold the true mean excess return 95 times in 100 if the observations were independent. They overlap, so the honest range is wider, and a range that spans zero has not shown an edge.
How many years of history sit behind the row, one observation for each year. A calendar month seen fifteen times is a small sample, which is why the bar for significance is raised.
How many trading days fall in the bucket over the history. More days make a real effect easier to tell apart from chance.
The average return per period in this bucket, in percent: per month in the monthly table and per day in the others. It is the raw figure, before the benchmark is taken off.
The same average with the benchmark's return over the same periods taken off. It separates this stock's own calendar effect from the market's.
The share of periods in the bucket that ended higher. It shows how consistent the effect is, which an average can hide.
The same mean with that month's single best year removed. A figure that collapses when one year comes out was one year, not a season.
The middle daily return in the bucket, with half the days above it and half below. Far from the mean means a few large days are carrying the average.
The p-value: how often a difference at least this large would turn up by chance if the calendar had no effect at all. A row counts only when it clears the corrected bar stated above the table.
Whether the row clears the significance bar after the correction for how many rows were tested. A row that fails may still look large, but it has not shown it is more than chance.
The stretch of each month the row covers: the turn of the month, meaning its last and first few trading days, or the rest of it. The window is fixed in advance, not chosen for its result.
The dollar value of the holdings mapped to this exposure. Funds that track the same thing are added together as one exposure.
This exposure's share of the whole portfolio's value today, in percent. Funds that track the same index count together as one exposure.
The share of the portfolio the example allocation gives this exposure, in percent. It is the example's weight, not a target for your money.
How far the current share sits from the example's, in percentage points. Positive means this exposure is a larger share than in the example, and negative a smaller one.

The part of this year's contribution that goes to this fund, in percent. New money goes to the exposures furthest below target, which moves the portfolio back toward the model without selling anything.

Optic's long-term trend model's reading of the stock, from a score built on its trend, valuation and record: high, moderate, neutral, cautious or low. With too little usable history the score is capped, so a short record cannot read as a strong one.
The long-term score behind the reading, from minus 100 to plus 100. The high reading starts at 40 and the low one at minus 40.
How many years of prices the figures are measured over. A short history may have missed a full market cycle, which flatters it.
The share of the model allocation this fund holds, in percent, or a dash when the model does not use it. The highlighted rows are the funds in the model.
The fund's annual expense ratio: the share of the money invested that the fund deducts each year to cover its costs. It comes out of the return every year, so small differences compound over decades.

The compound annual growth rate over the fund's full available history: the steady yearly return that would turn its first price into its latest. A fund with a short history is measured over fewer years, which makes its figure less comparable.
How much the fund's daily returns swing, annualised and in percent. Higher volatility means a bumpier ride, whatever the average return.

The full-history annual growth rate divided by the volatility: how much return each unit of swing has bought. It is a Sharpe ratio with the risk-free rate set to zero, so it compares funds with each other rather than with cash.
How many years of prices the figures are measured over. A short history may have missed a full market cycle, which flatters it.
The index's change over the past twelve months, in percent. A single year can sit far from the long-run rates beside it.

The long-term trend in words, from weekly closes against the 40-week and 200-week averages: secular uptrend, uptrend correcting, attempted bottom, secular downtrend or neutral. It moves slowly by design and says nothing about the next few weeks.
Profit or loss from the trades closed in the month, in dollars. An open position counts only once it closes, in the month it closes.
The month's realised profit or loss as a percentage of what the account was worth when the month began. Each month is measured against its own starting equity, not the original stake.
What the account was worth at the end of the month, counting closed trades only. It carries forward, so each month starts from where the one before it ended.
Calendar days until the contract expires. Fewer days means faster time decay and less room for the move to happen.
The midpoint between the bid and the ask, per share: an estimate of a fair fill, not a guaranteed price. A wide spread makes it less reliable.
What one contract costs at the estimated mid: the per-share premium times the 100 shares a contract covers. It is the figure that would leave the account.
The contract's return if the stock reaches the target by the estimated exit date, with implied volatility unchanged. It is repriced with an options model, so the time decay along the way is included.
The return at the target if implied volatility also falls by a fifth, as it often does after an event. A move can be right and the trade still lose to the fall in volatility.
The return if the stock is unchanged at the estimated exit date, so only time has passed. It is what the time decay alone costs, and it is the most common outcome.
The return if the stock moves half the distance to the target in the wrong direction by the exit date. It shows how quickly the contract loses when the read is wrong.
What the factor measures: the price trend, risk, valuation, income, timing or a resolved catalyst. Most of the points available come from how the price has behaved.
What this factor added to or took from the long-term score. The column adds up to the total underneath, which is capped between minus 100 and plus 100.

Profit or loss in multiples of what the trade was set up to lose: the distance from entry to stop, times the size. Plus 2R means it made twice what the stop would have cost, which holds whatever the account size.
Where the latest price came from: the last trade for shares, or the midpoint of the option chain for options. A mid is not a fill, so a real exit would pay some of the spread.
The stance Optic held on this symbol when the trade was opened, kept as it was. Comparing it with the result shows how trades with Optic's read fared against trades against it.

Earnings per share: the company's profit over the last twelve months divided by its shares. It is the figure the trailing P/E is calculated from, and a buyback can lift it even when profit does not grow.
The earnings per share analysts expect over the coming year, the average of their estimates. A forecast rather than a result, and the figure the forward P/E is calculated from.

A year of dividends at the current rate, as a percentage of the share price. 2% means about $2 a year for every $100 of stock, before tax. A yield also rises when the price falls, so a high one can be a warning rather than a gift.
The price the regular session opened at, 9:30am Eastern. The gap from the previous close is what moved overnight, on news or in other markets.
The highest price traded in the regular session, 9:30am to 4pm Eastern. Trades before the open or after the close are not counted, so a reaction to news after hours shows in the next session's range.
The lowest price traded in the regular session, 9:30am to 4pm Eastern. With the high, it is how far the stock swung in one day. Trades before the open or after the close are not counted.
How many shares changed hands in the regular session, so far if it is still open. Read against average volume: a move on heavy volume had many traders behind it, and one on light volume had few.
The average number of shares traded per day over the last three months. It is the yardstick for today's volume, and a guide to how easily the stock can be bought or sold without moving its price.

The highest price the stock traded at in the past 52 weeks, counting intraday highs rather than closing prices. Read with the 52-week low, it shows whether today's price is near the top of its year or the bottom.

The lowest price the stock traded at in the past 52 weeks, counting intraday lows rather than closing prices. Read with the 52-week high, it shows how wide the year's swings were and where today's price sits within them.

How far the stock has tended to move when the market moves, from five years of monthly returns against the S&P 500. 1 means in step with the market, 2 about twice as far either way, and below 1 less. It describes the past, and says nothing about direction.
Exchanges report it twice a month, so it is as of the date shown.

Net income as a percentage of revenue over the last twelve months. Of every dollar that came in, how many cents the company kept after every cost, including interest and tax. A one-off gain, such as selling part of the business, can lift it for a year.

How much revenue grew in the most recent quarter, against the same quarter a year earlier. Comparing like quarters takes out seasonal swings, and an acquisition can add growth the existing business did not earn.

How much the number of shares sold short changed since the previous report, about two weeks earlier. Rising means more is being bet against the stock; falling means short sellers have been buying back.
The number of shares sold short and not yet bought back, at the settlement date of the latest report. It is the count the percentage of float is worked out from.
Shares sold short at the previous report, about two weeks before the latest one. The baseline the change beside it is measured against.
The consensus: the earnings per share analysts expected for the quarter, averaged across their estimates before the report. It is the bar the result is judged against.

The earnings per share the company reported for the quarter, as the data source records it. It is not always on the same basis as the estimate, so a one-off gain or charge can turn an ordinary quarter into a huge beat or miss.
Revenue in the latest fiscal year against the year before, from the annual statements below. Annual figures move slowly, so a turn shows here after it has shown in the quarters.

Net income in the latest fiscal year against the year before. It is left out when the earlier year was a loss, because growth from a loss has no meaningful percentage, and one-off gains or charges move it far more than they move revenue.
This one is for the latest fiscal year.

Net income per share, counting the extra shares that options, convertible debt and other awards could create, as filed in the annual statement. The strictest per-share figure, and usually a little below basic EPS, which leaves those shares out.
Cash and cash equivalents on the latest annual balance sheet: money in the bank and holdings that turn into cash almost at once. What the company could spend without selling anything or borrowing.

Everything the company has borrowed, short and long term, on the latest annual balance sheet, including lease obligations where they are reported as debt. A company with no loans can still show some, from its leases.
Cash minus total debt. Positive means the cash on hand would cover everything owed; negative means the company owes more than it holds, which is net debt.
It turns negative when years of buybacks or losses have pushed shareholders' equity below zero, and then no longer reads as a measure of leverage.
This is the latest fiscal year, from the annual statement.

EBITDA as a percentage of revenue: of every dollar of sales, how many cents were left before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Above the operating margin by the depreciation and amortisation it leaves out, so the gap is widest at capital-heavy companies.

Shares the company's directors and officers bought, minus shares they sold, over the last six months, from their Form 4 filings. Positive means they were net buyers, the rarer and more telling direction.
From their quarterly 13F filings, which arrive up to 45 days after the quarter they cover.

Of the largest reported holders, how many raised their stake by more than 2% at their last quarterly filing, and how many cut it by more than 2%. The filings arrive up to 45 days after the quarter they describe.

Shares the company's directors and officers bought over the last six months, and in how many trades. Buying with their own money is the more telling direction, because there is only one reason to do it.
Shares the company's directors and officers sold over the last six months, and in how many trades. Much of it is scheduled in advance or covers tax on vested shares, so it says less than buying does.
The share of the company's stock owned by its directors, officers and largest owners. A high figure means management's own money rides on the price, and fewer shares are free to trade.
The number of shares the holder reported owning at its last quarterly filing. Index funds own most large companies in proportion to their size, so the biggest names on this list are often passive.
The holder's stake as a share of all the company's shares, as of its last filing. Funds file quarterly, so the figure can be months old.
How many shares the transaction covered, as the insider reported it on Form 4. Awards, gifts and option exercises are listed too, as Other, not only purchases and sales.
The dollar value the filing gives for the transaction. A dash means none was stated, which is usual for awards, gifts and option exercises.
How much the holder's position grew or shrank at its latest filing, against the one before. Index funds change with their index, so their moves say less than an active manager's.
The most recent dividend per share, dated by its ex-dividend date: a buyer on or after that day does not receive it. The payment itself usually arrives a few weeks later.

How many complete calendar years in a row the yearly dividend total has risen, and the last year it fell. A long streak is a habit of raising, not a promise to keep doing it. It is counted from the data source's record by ex-dividend date, so a payment doubled or missing there can read as a cut.
Dividends per share across the last complete calendar year, counted by ex-dividend date. A special one-off payment lifts it for that year only.
How many dividend payments the data source holds for the company, back to the earliest it has. The table below shows the most recent of them.
Dividends per share for that calendar year, counted by ex-dividend date. A year with a special payment stands out against its neighbours.
The year's total against the year before, as a percentage. A cut shows here first, and the growth streak is the run of positive years at the top.

How many shares each one became: 4-for-1 means every share turned into four, each worth a quarter as much. Below 1 is a reverse split, which merges shares; either way the company's value is unchanged.

The share of the stock's off-exchange trading on the latest day that FINRA's daily file reports as short sales. Market makers selling short to fill buy orders are counted, so a high reading is often routine liquidity rather than bets against the stock.
The same share averaged over the days on record: this stock's own normal. A day is unusual against this, not against 50%, because market making keeps the level high for most stocks.
The latest day's share minus the average, in percentage points. A day well away from the stock's own normal says more than the level itself does.
How many trading days of FINRA's daily files the average covers, up to the last twenty. FINRA publishes one file for each trading day, usually that evening.

The average of analysts' estimates of earnings per share for the coming report, with the lowest and highest beside it. A wide range means they disagree, and a bigger surprise either way is more likely.

The average of analysts' revenue estimates for the coming report, with the lowest and highest beside it. Revenue is harder to flatter than earnings, so a miss here can matter more than an earnings beat.

The move the options market is pricing through the report: an at-the-money call plus put at the first expiry after it, as a share of the price. It is the breakeven move, so it slightly understates the move the market expects.
Counted over the quarters shown here, and a quarter exactly in line counts against it.

How far the stock moved in the session that reacted to the report: the report day itself when it came out before the open, the next day when it came out after the close. A session still trading is not counted until it ends.

The stock's move in after-hours or pre-market trading since the report, against the last regular close. Far fewer shares trade then, so it is the market's first read and can retrace once the regular session opens.

What the stock has really done over a comparable stretch. When the expiry is within a week of the report, the average move in the sessions that reacted to past reports; otherwise the average move over windows as long as the option's life, across the past two years.

The implied move divided by the actual one. At 1.25 or above the options cost more than the stock's own record would justify, at 0.85 or below less, and in between they are fairly priced by this measure.
This one is for the at-the-money option at the expiry above, as a yearly rate.
Analysts' current average estimate of earnings per share for that period: this quarter, next quarter, this fiscal year or next. The columns beside it show how the estimate has moved.

How much that estimate has changed in the last 30 days, as a share of what it was then. Estimates usually move after the company's own guidance, so this is the closest free read of what management said.
The same change over 90 days. Three months of revisions is a steadier read than one, and the full-year rows decide whether estimates are called rising or falling.
How many analysts raised their estimate for that period in the last 30 days, and how many cut it. Several moving the same way says more than the size of any one change.
The average gap between reported EPS and consensus across the quarters below, as a percentage of the estimate. One quarter with a one-off gain or charge can dominate it.
The average size of the stock's move in the sessions that reacted to the reports below, up or down. It is the yardstick for a straddle that expires within a week of the next report.
The stock's average move in the reacting session after the quarters it beat consensus. Negative means beats have been sold, so the bar the market cares about sits above the consensus.
The stock's average move in the reacting session after the quarters it missed or only matched consensus. A small figure means a miss was expected, or did not matter to the price.
This quarter's revenue against the same quarter a year earlier, which takes out seasonal swings. The free feed carries five quarters of statements, so only the latest quarter has one.
This quarter's net income against the same quarter a year earlier. It is left out when that earlier quarter was a loss, because growth from a loss has no meaningful percentage.
The fiscal year's revenue against the year before, from the annual statements. Annual figures move slowly, so a turn shows in the quarters first.
The fiscal year's net income against the year before. It is left out when that earlier year was a loss, because growth from a loss has no meaningful percentage.
Analysts' average estimate of earnings per share for that period: this quarter, next quarter, this fiscal year or next. A forecast rather than a result.
How far that estimate is above or below earnings for the same period a year earlier, as the data source reports it. From a loss a year earlier, the percentage says little.
Analysts' average revenue estimate for that period. Revenue is harder to flatter than earnings, so its estimate is the steadier of the two.
How far the revenue estimate is above or below revenue for the same period a year earlier, as the data source reports it. Comparing like periods takes out seasonal swings.
How many analysts' estimates go into the earnings average for that period. The fewer there are, the less a consensus it is, and the more one estimate can move it.

The average of the price targets analysts have published, usually for twelve months out, with the lowest and highest beside it. A sentiment gauge more than a forecast: targets sit above the price in almost every market.
How far the mean target is above or below today's price. A wide gap means either the targets are stale or the market disagrees with them.
The share of analysts rating the stock a buy or strong buy this month. When nearly all of them already do, an upgrade has little room left to move the price.

How many analysts rate the stock a buy, a hold or a sell this month, with strong ratings counted in with the plain ones. Sell ratings are rare, so holds carry more of the doubt than the name suggests.
Now is this month's count of ratings; -1m, -2m and -3m are the counts one, two and three months ago. Read down the rows to see which way opinion is moving.

Optic's combined short-term reading of four inputs (the chart trend, dealer gamma, options activity and news tone) as one score.
A quick summary of whether the signals Optic tracks lean up or down over the next 2 to 8 weeks, and how strongly they agree.
Above the midpoint leans bullish, below it bearish. The conviction word says how strong and how consistent the inputs are; near the middle means they are weak or disagree.
It is not a forecast or a price target, and Optic shows its track record only where it has measured one. It cannot see news it has not received.
An estimate of how much stock options dealers would have to buy or sell to stay hedged as the price moves, added up across every strike. Traders call it gamma exposure, or GEX.
That hedging can be large enough to calm a stock or to speed it up, so it is used to judge whether moves are likely to be orderly or sharp.
Positive: dealer hedging tends to sell into rises and buy into falls, which can damp swings. Negative: hedging adds to moves in both directions. The flip point is the price where it changes sign.
Nobody reports dealer positions. The figure rests on an assumption about which side of each contract dealers hold, so it is a model, and it is wrong whenever that assumption is.
How much dealers' hedging would change if options got cheaper or dearer (implied volatility moving) while the share price stood still. Traders call it vanna exposure, or VEX.
Option prices often fall after an event such as earnings, and the hedging that follows can push the stock even with no news.
The larger the figure, the more a change in option prices would shift hedging. Its sign comes from the same dealer assumption as gamma, so read it beside that panel.
A second-order estimate on top of an assumption about who holds each contract. It describes pressure that might arise, not trades that have happened.
How much the options open on this stock would gain or lose for a $1 move in the share price, added up across calls and puts (delta).
It shows whether the options market as a whole is positioned for the price to rise or to fall.
Positive net delta means the open positions gain if the price rises; negative means they gain if it falls.
Open interest counts contracts, not who holds them or why. A large put position can be insurance on shares someone owns rather than a bet against the company.
How fast the options' delta changes as the price moves, strike by strike (gamma).
Strikes with heavy gamma are where hedging is busiest, so the price can stall or speed up around them.
The tallest bars mark the strikes that matter most to hedging. The call and put walls are the largest concentrations above and below the price.
The same dealer-position assumption as gamma exposure. A wall is where hedging is heaviest, not a floor or a ceiling the price must respect.
Activity in calls (which pay if the price rises) against puts (which pay if it falls), weighted by volume and open interest, and the dollars spent at each strike.
A lean toward calls or toward puts shows which way options traders are positioning.
A put/call ratio below 1 means more call activity than put activity, above 1 the reverse. Bars above zero mean more was spent on calls at that strike.
The free data has no record of individual trades, so Optic cannot tell buyers from sellers. Heavy put activity can be shareholders buying protection rather than betting on a fall.
The Relative Strength Index: the size of recent up days against down days over the last 14 sessions, on a scale of 0 to 100.
A common way to see whether a move has been unusually one-sided.
By convention, above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold, and around 50 neutral.
In a strong trend a stock can stay above 70 or below 30 for weeks. It describes the last 14 sessions and does not predict a reversal.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence: the gap between the 12-day and 26-day average prices, and a 9-day average of that gap, called the signal line.
Traders watch it for momentum turning up or down.
MACD above its signal line suggests momentum is improving, below it that momentum is fading. The bars show the distance between the two.
Built from past prices, so it lags turns. In a sideways market it crosses back and forth with nothing following.
The share price with its averages over recent periods and the common pullback (Fibonacci) levels drawn on.
It shows the trend at a glance and where earlier moves paused.
A price above a rising 200-day average is usually called an uptrend; shorter averages above longer ones confirm it.
Averages describe the past and turn late. Fibonacci levels are a trading convention, not a law the price follows.
Example option trades Optic builds from the current reading, with their cost, most you could lose and break-even price.
They show how a view on the stock could be expressed with options, and what it would cost.
Costs are for one contract, which covers 100 shares. Break-even is where the trade stops losing money at expiry.
Examples for study, not recommendations. An option can lose its whole value, and the prices here are delayed.
How expensive this stock's options are (implied volatility) against their own past year and against how much the stock has actually been moving.
It tells you whether buying options is cheap or dear by this stock’s own standard.
A high IV rank means options cost more than usual for this stock; a low one, less.
Implied volatility is the price of uncertainty, not a forecast of direction or of the size of the next move.
How the stock has done in each calendar month across past years.
Some businesses and markets have recurring calendar patterns, for example around reporting seasons.
Each month shows its average return and how often it was positive.
A handful of years can produce a pattern by chance, and a past calendar pattern is weak evidence about this year.
Shapes in recent price history that traders give names to, such as triangles or double tops, found by fixed rules.
Some traders use them to time entries and exits.
Each pattern lists its level and, where Optic has measured it, how often that pattern was followed by a move.
Patterns fail often, and finding one after the fact is easier than acting on it.

The move the options market is pricing for the earnings report (the implied move), against how much the stock has actually moved after past reports.
It shows whether options look expensive or cheap for the event.
A ratio above 1 means options are pricing a bigger move than the stock has usually made; below 1, a smaller one.
The implied move is about size, not direction, and any single report can move the stock far more or less.
How analysts' forecasts of earnings have changed over the last 30 and 90 days.
Rising estimates often follow good news from the company itself.
More analysts raising than cutting is the favourable direction.
Analysts often move together and can be wrong together.
Shares sold short, borrowed and sold by investors betting on a fall, as a share of the shares available to trade, and how many days of normal trading it would take to buy them back.
It shows how many investors are betting against the stock.
A higher percentage means more bets against. More days to cover means short sellers would take longer to get out, which can make rises sharper.
Reported twice a month and about two weeks late. Some short selling is hedging rather than a bet against the company.
Shares bought and sold by the company's own directors and officers, and the stakes of large funds, from their required filings.
Insiders know the business best, and big funds move prices.
Insider buying is the more telling direction. Fund stakes rising suggests demand from large holders.
Much insider selling is planned in advance or pays tax on awarded shares, and fund filings arrive up to 45 days after the quarter.
One risk-on or risk-off reading built from volatility, the dollar, interest rates, commodities, credit and crypto.
Most stocks move with the wider market, so it helps to know whether conditions favour taking risk.
Risk-on means those markets are behaving in a way that has tended to suit stocks; risk-off, the opposite.
A label on recent data, not a forecast. Turning points are only clear afterwards.
How many stocks are rising against falling, and how many are above their own averages.
It shows whether a market move is broad or carried by a few large companies.
Broad participation supports a rally; narrow breadth means a handful of names are doing the work.
Breadth can stay narrow for a long time while the index keeps rising.
Which sectors are gaining or losing ground against the S&P 500.
Money moving between sectors can be a sign of what investors expect from the economy.
Sectors improving and ahead of the market are leading; those falling behind are lagging.
Leadership can change quickly, and recent strength is no promise of more.

The inflation print the Fed's 2% mandate is written against. Rate expectations for the next two meetings usually reset within seconds of the release, which is why it moves the whole index and not just rate-sensitive sectors. Core (stripping food and energy) is what gets traded; the headline number is noisier because of petrol.

Prices at the factory gate, before anything reaches a shop shelf. Read as a leading indicator for CPI and as a direct read on margins: a producer absorbing higher input costs is a producer with a thinner margin next quarter.

Payrolls and the unemployment rate. The other half of the Fed's dual mandate. Average hourly earnings inside the same release is the part that ties employment back to inflation, so a strong jobs number with soft wages reads very differently from a strong one with hot wages.

Vacancies and the quit rate. Quits are the honest signal. People leave jobs when they are confident of finding a better one, so the rate falls before payrolls do. Slower and less traded than the jobs report, but it turns earlier.

The Fed's preferred wage measure, because it holds the mix of jobs constant. Average hourly earnings can fall simply because low-paid hiring picked up; this one cannot. Quarterly, so each print carries three months of information.

Wages after inflation. Whether pay packets actually bought more. Derived from CPI and the jobs report, both already released, so it very rarely moves a price. It matters for the consumer-demand story rather than for the tape.

Output per hour, and unit labour costs. This is the release that decides whether wage growth is inflationary: pay rising alongside productivity can be absorbed, pay rising without it lands in prices or margins.

Traded-goods prices, which is where the dollar shows up in inflation. A strong dollar makes imports cheaper and quietly does some of the Fed's work; a weak one does the opposite. Mostly a second-order read on CPI.
Local labour-market detail, published with a long lag. Useful for regional analysis and essentially never a market event.
The state-level breakdown of a national number already published. Included for completeness; it does not move an index.

The record of the last meeting's discussion, published three weeks after it. The decision is already known, so what can move prices is the detail: how many officials leaned toward the next change and what they said about inflation and the balance sheet. Usually smaller than the decision itself; it matters when the discussion reads more hawkish or dovish than the statement and press conference did.

The rate decision itself, plus the statement and, at four of the eight meetings, the projections and a press conference. The decision is usually priced well in advance, so the move tends to come from the language and the dot plot rather than the number, and often from the press conference rather than the statement.
